design_detail: Editorial (Addiction, pp. 726–727; ten paragraphs, 19 references) by six alcohol epidemiologists arguing that observed health benefits of low-volume (‘moderate’) drinking reflect confounding and selection bias from how abstainers are defined, and are contradicted by Mendelian randomization (MR) studies; it recommends that burden-of-disease estimates, drinking guidelines, clinicians and policy no longer assume protective effects. No search, selection criteria, data or synthesis. Appraised with the editors' narrative-review checklist, as the round brief directs for commentaries and debate pieces.
can_establish: Which arguments and sources a group of alcohol epidemiologists relied on in January 2015 to doubt protective effects of low-volume drinking, and the policy recommendations they drew from them.
cannot_establish: Whether low-volume drinking lowers or raises mortality or cardiovascular risk; how complete or strong the cited evidence is (no search, no appraisal, no quantitative synthesis); or the accuracy of its summaries of other studies, which must be checked against those studies.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (editorial). The 19 cited sources: a Swedish societal-cost study; a cardiology paper and the Ronksley et al. (2011) meta-analysis, cited together as arguing for a therapeutic role of alcohol; a critique of J-shaped findings (Fekjaer, 2013); confounder and selection-bias studies (Naimi et al., 2005; Ng Fat & Shelton, 2012; Fillmore et al., 2006; Liang & Chikritzhs, 2013); eight Mendelian randomization or genetic studies (refs 9 to 16: Holmes et al., 2014, and others on cognition, child academic achievement, balance, blood pressure and cardiovascular biomarkers); two observational studies of intima-media thickness and coronary calcification in young adults; and a Mediterranean-diet trial (Estruch et al., 2013).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria; sources chosen by the authors.
sample.selection_effects: Selection is the authors' own and one-directional: no study reporting benefit is examined, Ronksley et al. being cited only as having led others to see alcohol as therapeutic. Three of the 19 references come from the authors' own group and carry the abstainer-bias argument (Naimi et al., 2005, with Naimi; Fillmore et al., 2006, with Stockwell and Chikritzhs; Liang & Chikritzhs, 2013). One cited MR source is an unrefereed working paper, and two of the four sources cited as further MR studies concern prenatal alcohol exposure and children's outcomes, according to their titles.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. ‘Moderate’ drinking is glossed as low average volume; the description of Holmes et al. mentions a cut-off of 21 g of ethanol a day.

comparison.controls: Not applicable. The argument concerns the abstainer reference group of cohort studies, said to be inflated by former and occasional drinkers with poorer health.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable. Outcomes discussed: cardiovascular disease and coronary heart disease (CHD), stroke, type 2 diabetes, all-cause mortality, cognitive function, children's academic achievement and balance, blood pressure, HDL cholesterol, C-reactive protein, fibrinogen, coronary calcification and carotid intima-media thickness.
outcomes.operationalization: Protection is framed as lower risk in low-volume drinkers than in abstainers; MR evidence is treated as closer to randomization than cohort evidence.

analysis.effect_sizes: None. The editorial reports no estimates from the studies it cites; the only number is the 21 g/day cut-off it attributes to Holmes et al.
analysis.selective_reporting: Evidence for protective associations is mentioned only to be set aside; limitations of the MR studies, and of the observational studies cited in support (intima-media thickness, coronary calcification), are not discussed.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Four lines of argument, each resting on a few cited studies: protective associations have been reported for implausible conditions (liver cirrhosis, fetal effects, the common cold); confounding and the counting of former and occasional drinkers as abstainers can produce the J-curve (Fillmore et al., 2006; Liang & Chikritzhs, 2013); MR studies, chiefly Holmes et al. (2014), find no benefit of low-volume drinking; and MR studies suggest HDL cholesterol, C-reactive protein and fibrinogen are not causal for CHD, while intima-media thickness and coronary calcification rise with drinking.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The editorial concludes, explicitly as the authors' opinion, that the field is due for a major repositioning, invokes the precautionary principle in the absence of randomized studies (Mendelian or clinical) supporting benefit, and recommends that burden-of-disease estimates and guidelines assume no protective effect, that guidelines discourage drinking for health reasons, that clinicians not recommend moderate drinking, and that the benefit hypothesis play no role in policy. Gaps: (1) the title's collapse and the conclusion rest on a handful of studies chosen without search; (2) one MR meta-analysis is presented as closer to a randomized trial than to cohort studies without examining whether the instrument assumptions hold for alcohol variants (effects of the variant other than through the amount drunk, or analyses split by drinking status, which the variant itself influences): the editorial states the exclusion assumption but does not test it; (3) observational associations in the harmful direction (intima-media thickness, coronary calcification) are accepted at face value while those in the protective direction are attributed to bias; (4) showing that three biomarkers are not causal for CHD rules out those pathways, not protection through others, and the statement that any mortality benefit runs through cardiovascular outcomes is uncited; (5) a diet trial that did not randomize alcohol cannot show that wine has no effect; (6) two of the MR examples concern prenatal exposure, not adult low-volume drinking. The recommendations not to assume benefit and not to advise drinking for health can be defended on precautionary grounds whether or not the hypothesis has collapsed.

timeline.event: Naimi et al.: potential confounders of heart disease more common among US non-drinkers than moderate drinkers (cited; Naimi is a co-author of this editorial).
Fillmore et al.: meta-analysis grouping studies by abstainer definition (cited; Stockwell and Chikritzhs co-authored it).
Ronksley et al. meta-analysis of cardiovascular outcomes, cited as an example of the protective reading (carded in this round by another reader).
Holmes et al. Mendelian randomization meta-analysis, the editorial's central evidence (carded in this round by another reader).
This editorial (first published 22 January 2015); no linked comments are listed on PubMed.
Stockwell et al. meta-analysis by three of the same authors, which cites this editorial in its first sentence (card sc_stockwell_2016, this round).

On the project list: the GBD 2016 alcohol analysis (Griswold et al.), described there as the ‘no safe level’ paper; how it treated the protective effects this editorial asked burden estimates to drop is for its own card (carded in this round by another reader).
On the project list: Mukamal, Stampfer and Rimm's critique of Mendelian randomization studies of alcohol and cardiovascular disease (not read).
Zhao et al. update of the abstainer-referenced meta-analysis, with Stockwell and Naimi as authors (card sc_zhao_2023, this round).

replication.where_it_stands: A position statement that framed the later debate rather than evidence in its own right. Each of its factual claims should be cited from the primary study it summarizes, several of which are carded in this round; the Mendelian randomization evidence and its published critique are appraised separately.

funding.affiliations_note: National Drug Research Institute, Curtin University (Chikritzhs, Liang); Centre for Addictions Research of BC, University of Victoria (Stockwell); Boston Medical Center (Naimi); Karolinska Institutet (Andreasson); Sahlgrenska Academy and University Hospital, Gothenburg (Dangardt). Three authors wrote the abstainer-bias studies the editorial relies on, and three later wrote the 2016 meta-analysis that tests its claim. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Not answerable by an editorial. The question it raises would be settled by a long-term randomized trial of low-volume drinking against abstention, or by genetic analyses able to estimate the dose–response at low intake without splitting participants by drinking status, together with cohort analyses using lifetime abstainers and lifetime drinking histories.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria; 19 sources chosen by the authors.
No appraisal of any cited study; an unrefereed working paper and prenatal-exposure studies are cited as MR evidence on low-dose drinking without comment.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Three of 19 references are from the authors' group, and they carry the abstainer-bias argument; the MR evidence comes from other groups.

The conclusion is labelled as opinion and the recommendations as recommendations, but contested inferences (MR as near-randomized, the biomarker argument, the diet-trial inference) are stated as findings.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against protective effects of low-volume drinking
domains.note: Only evidence against protection is presented; the evidence for it (cohort meta-analyses, experimental biomarker studies) is mentioned only to be dismissed, and the limitations of MR are not discussed, so the case for benefit is under-represented.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard instrument applies to an editorial (METHODS §5.3). It is a clearly argued advocacy piece whose selection is unsystematic and one-sided and whose cited studies are not appraised; the overall judgment follows the worst domains. Claims should cite the primary studies it summarizes and may cite this editorial only for the position its authors took in 2015 and for its recommendations, attributed to them (for example that guidelines should discourage drinking for health reasons).

key_findings.finding: The summary line states that evolving epidemiological evidence, including better methods for assessing causality, is raising doubts about whether moderate drinking protects health.

The authors say protective estimates for heart disease, stroke and type 2 diabetes have been built into international burden-of-disease estimates, including the Global Burden of Disease project, into some national drinking guidelines and into economic cost estimates, and have led some authors to propose alcohol as a therapeutic agent for some patients.

The authors argue that protective associations are unlikely to be causal because they have been reported for implausible conditions (liver cirrhosis, fetal effects, the common cold), and that confounding and selection bias contribute to the J-shaped curve.

Fillmore et al. (2006) are summarized as finding no significant protection in studies that kept former and occasional drinkers out of the abstainer group, explained by people quitting or cutting down as they age and fall ill; Liang and Chikritzhs (2013) are summarized as removing the difference in health status between abstainers and low-dose drinkers by combining former with current drinkers and adjusting for confounding.

MR is described as using genetic variants associated with exposure but not with typical confounders, assuming the genotype affects the outcome only through the exposure; Holmes et al. (2014) are summarized as showing lower cardiovascular risk in drinkers carrying a variant linked to lower consumption, in a sentence that also refers to people consuming up to 21 g of ethanol a day, with the association seen in drinkers but not in non-drinkers. The authors write that MR “resembles more closely a randomized controlled trial (RCT) than traditional observational studies”.
key_findings.note: The editorial's sentence on Holmes et al. is ambiguously worded (see reporting issues); check the primary study before citing the 21 g/day subgroup.

key_findings.finding: Further MR studies are cited as finding no protective effect of low-dose alcohol on cognitive function, children's academic achievement, balance and blood pressure.
key_findings.note: By their titles, refs 11 and 12 concern prenatal alcohol exposure and children's outcomes, and ref 11 is a National Bureau of Economic Research working paper.

key_findings.finding: MR studies are cited as suggesting that HDL cholesterol, C-reactive protein and fibrinogen are not causally related to CHD, and observational studies as showing only positive associations of drinking with coronary calcification and carotid intima-media thickness; the authors conclude that these biomarkers cannot explain an apparent protective effect on all-cause mortality, which they say is driven by cardiovascular outcomes.
A trial of a Mediterranean diet (Estruch et al., 2013), not randomized for alcohol, is cited as suggesting that the French paradox may reflect diet rather than wine.

In the authors' stated opinion the foundations of the protective hypothesis are so undermined that the field is due for repositioning; they invoke the precautionary principle in the absence of randomized studies, Mendelian or clinical, supporting protective effects.

Recommendations: future burden-of-disease estimates, including the Global Burden of Disease, and national guidelines should assume no protective effect of low-dose drinking; guidelines should discourage drinking for health reasons; health professionals should not recommend moderate drinking to reduce cardiovascular risk; the hypothesis of health benefits should play no role in policy decisions.
Declaration of interests: none. No funding statement. Six authors, 19 references.
key_findings.locator: Declaration of interests; author information; References

reporting_issues.issue: The sentence summarizing Holmes et al. is ambiguous: it says drinkers with a variant linked to lower consumption among those consuming up to 21 g a day had decreased cardiovascular risk, leaving unclear whether 21 g/day defines a subgroup of the analysis or describes the carriers' intake.
reporting_issues.consequence: The editorial cannot be cited for what Holmes et al. found at low intake; the primary study (carded by another reader) must be used.

reporting_issues.issue: Two of the four sources cited as further MR studies showing no benefit of low-dose alcohol (refs 11 and 12) concern prenatal exposure and children's academic achievement or balance, according to their titles; ref 11 is an unrefereed working paper, and the title of ref 12 does not identify an MR design.
reporting_issues.consequence: These sources do not bear on adult low-volume drinking and should not be counted as MR evidence on it.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that any positive mortality effect of low-dose drinking is driven by cardiovascular outcomes, on which the biomarker argument depends, has no citation.
reporting_issues.consequence: The step from non-causal biomarkers to no mortality benefit is the authors' assertion.

reporting_issues.issue: Several author names in the reference list are garbled: Ronksley is given the initial R (ref 3), and George Davey Smith appears as Davey S. G. (refs 13 and 14) and Dave S. G. (ref 16).
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; match references by DOI, not by author name.
